idiom_name: EF Core table-per-hierarchy (TPH) with the Discriminator column
implementation_notes: Entity Framework Core maps a CLR hierarchy with table-per-hierarchy by default: one table for all types plus a discriminator column that EF creates implicitly as a shadow property, with derived properties made nullable automatically. HasDiscriminator(...) configures the column name/type and one value per type (HasValue<T>), and IsComplete(false) tells EF to keep applying the discriminator predicate even for values that are not in the model. The DbContext/DbSet is the mapper layer; the manual form (Dapper/ADO.NET plus a switch on the discriminator) is only worth writing when you deliberately avoid EF's change tracking.
pitfalls: EF maps only types you tell it about: a subclass with neither a DbSet nor explicit model configuration is not in the hierarchy, and rows whose discriminator names it become unmaterialisable.

Materialising a row whose discriminator is not in the model throws; after importing data from elsewhere either map the extra type or mark the discriminator IsComplete(false) so queries always filter by type.
Derived properties are nullable by construction, so required relationships or unique indexes on subtype-only columns need filtered indexes or CHECK constraints mirroring the discriminator.
The discriminator is a shadow property by default, so LINQ queries cannot portably reference it for projections or filters unless it is mapped to a real property.
